title: Punjab CM Mann Reverses Course, Now Backs Parole for Beant Singh's Assassin
excerpt: After years of opposing Jagtar Singh Hawara's release, the AAP government in Punjab has shifted its position, seeking 10-day parole for the man convicted of assassinating former Chief Minister Beant Singh.
body:
• Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann has reversed his government's position on Jagtar Singh Hawara, now seeking 10-day parole for the man convicted of assassinating former Punjab CM Beant Singh in 1995.
  • The Punjab government had previously opposed Hawara's transfer and parole in the Supreme Court, with the state's Advocate General arguing against his release.
  • Hawara has served 29 years in Mandoli Jail with a clean conduct record and has never been granted parole or remission.
  • The Punjab and Haryana High Court set a seven-week deadline in July 2026 for authorities to decide on Hawara's parole plea, filed on humanitarian grounds to care for his 81-year-old ailing mother.

Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann's government has made a striking reversal on the case of Jagtar Singh Hawara, the man serving a life sentence for the 1995 assassination of former Punjab Chief Minister Beant Singh. After years of opposing Hawara's release in court, the AAP-led state government is now seeking 10-day parole for the convicted assassin.

From Opposition to Advocacy

The shift marks a dramatic U-turn. As recently as early 2025, Punjab's Advocate General Gurminder Singh argued forcefully against Hawara in the Supreme Court, opposing his plea to be transferred from Delhi's Tihar Jail to a prison in Punjab. The AG contended that Hawara's earlier transfer plea had already been dismissed by the Delhi High Court in 2018 and that the Punjab prison manual did not apply to his case.

Now, according to recent reports, the Mann government has reversed that stance and is actively supporting Hawara's plea for temporary release — drawing both praise and sharp criticism across the political spectrum.

The 1995 Assassination

Hawara, a member of militant group Babbar Khalsa, was convicted for masterminding the assassination of Chief Minister Beant Singh on August 31, 1995. Beant Singh was killed in a suicide bomb attack at the Punjab Civil Secretariat in Chandigarh during a period of intense counter-insurgency operations against Sikh militants.

A CBI investigation led to Hawara's conviction under the IPC and the Explosive Substances Act. He was sentenced to death in 2007, but the Punjab and Haryana High Court commuted the sentence to life imprisonment in 2010. Appeals remain pending before the Supreme Court.

"Despite serving an actual custody period of 29 years with clean prison conduct, his client has never been granted parole."

— Senior Advocate Maninder Singh, representing Hawara

High Court Sets Deadline

On July 6, 2026, a division bench of the Punjab and Haryana High Court set a strict seven-week deadline for a decision on Hawara's parole application. He had sought four weeks of parole to care for his 81-year-old mother, citing her rapidly deteriorating health.

His lawyers argued that of 36 cases registered against Hawara, he had been acquitted or discharged in most — with only the assassination conviction remaining. The application had been stalled by a jurisdictional tangle: Mandoli Jail authorities mistakenly forwarded the file to Punjab instead of the UT Chandigarh, which has actual jurisdiction since the conviction was by a Chandigarh court.

Political Timing

Mann's reversal comes as Punjab's assembly elections, originally scheduled for February 2027, may be advanced to November 2026, according to AAP national convener Arvind Kejriwal. With the Sikh vote crucial to AAP's prospects, the government's new posture on Hawara — a figure who commands deep sympathy among segments of the Sikh community — has been widely read as electoral positioning.

Hawara's case has also drawn comparisons with the repeated parole grants given to Dera Sacha Sauda chief Gurmeet Ram Rahim Singh, convicted of rape and murder. Critics have pointed to a perceived double standard — one high-profile convict receiving regular temporary releases while Hawara has not received a single day of parole in nearly three decades. Panchayat bodies across Punjab have passed at least 66 resolutions supporting his parole.

Diaspora Resonance

The case resonates deeply with Sikh communities in the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom, where Hawara's imprisonment is viewed through the lens of the broader 1984 narrative — Operation Blue Star, the anti-Sikh riots, and decades of unresolved grievances. The Mann government's shift may ease political pressure from Sikh organizations abroad, though it risks alienating those who view any concession as a threat to Punjab's hard-won stability.

The seven-week clock set by the High Court means a decision on Hawara's parole is expected by late August 2026. Delhi Prison Rules state that parole is ordinarily not granted to convicts involved in terrorist activities or prison escape cases — a potential obstacle given Hawara's 2004 escape from custody.
